P01.explanation: The marsh takes in the farm creek's fertilizer nitrate and sends a third less of it on to the bay, so it is the bay's "kidney": it removes a dissolved waste from the water passing through it. "Net" fails because the outgoing water ran just as brown with mud as what came in, so the marsh was not catching what the water carried in suspension. "Lung" fails because the water left holding the same oxygen as the bay, so the marsh added none. "Kitchen" fails because the shrimp just outside the channel were living on plankton, not on marsh grass, so the bay's animals were not being fed from the marsh.

P02.explanation: "Cowed" fits: the pack killed few elk, yet the herd stopped lingering in the thickets, stayed watchful while feeding, and kept doing so even when the wolves were thirty miles off, so the wolves changed the herd's behavior through fear. "Chased" fails because the elk avoided the thickets in weeks when no wolf was near them, so no pursuit was pushing them out. "Ambushed" fails because most kills were on the open benches, away from the thickets that could have hidden a wolf. "Corralled" fails because the elk fed in scattered bands across the benches, so they were spread out rather than confined.

P03.explanation: The meadows held half as many elk, collared elk died there at wolf kills while the survivors stayed put, and the slopes gained none, so the missing elk had not gone elsewhere: the wolves "reduced" the herd. "Redistributed" fails because the surviving collared cows kept to the same meadows and the slopes were no fuller, so where the herd lived did not change. "Rattled" fails because the survivors grazed heads down, as unhurried as elk filmed before the wolves, so their behavior was undisturbed. "Rejuvenated" fails because most of the dead were first-winter calves, which made the herd older, not younger.

P04.explanation: Spring winds drove sand off the dunes and across the village, the walls facing them were scoured to bare brick every year, and the palms on that side fruited only on their sheltered side, so the sand had "lashed" the village, striking it again and again. "Nibbled" fails because every house and garden of 1700 was still in use in 1900; the walls were scoured and replastered, but the village gave up no piece of itself. "Lifted" fails because the wind carried the sand on to the plain, and the doorways still stand at their builders' height, so the ground never rose. "Imprisoned" fails because caravans kept reaching the eastern gate.

P05.explanation: "Corridor" fits: young voles enter the strip, keep moving along it, and some reach the far forest, and the two forests' voles now share genes, so the strip carries animals between the forests. "Cafeteria" fails because the voles do not visit to eat and return home; marked animals moved on and ended up twelve miles away. "Cage" fails because voles that are rarely caught twice in one place and reach the other forest are not confined. "Cemetery" fails because voles in the strip live as long as voles in the forests, so the strip is not where they die.

P06.explanation: "Canteen" fits: parrotfish spend an hour each day with their beaks to the rock, and algae grows long only where mesh keeps them off, so they come to the outcrop to eat its algae. "Clinic" fails because the fish move along the rock working it with their beaks and pass the shrimp by; what changes is the algae they crop, not anything removed from them. "Bedroom" fails because the water around the outcrop empties at dusk. "Ballroom" fails because the schools come every day, feed and leave, with no seasonal gathering or courtship.

P07.explanation: Sentences from the mother's letters to her sister were set word for word into the diary's entries with no mark at the join, so the daughter joined material from a second source into the diary: she "spliced" it. "Tightened" means made more concise, but the book runs a fifth longer than the notebooks. "Tidied" means cleaned up the writing, but the misspellings were printed as written. "Softened" means toned down, but even the curses written after quarrels are printed.

P08.explanation: The villagers spread out in a line, drove every pony on the common into the village yard, and each family then claimed its own by ear notches, so the walk was a "roundup": gathering scattered livestock to be sorted and claimed. "Pilgrimage" fails because they turned at the boundary stone without stopping, so the far edge was only the point to sweep back from, not a place they went to honor. "Pageant" fails because they went in their oldest work clothes and did nothing for anyone to watch; the day was work. "Raid" fails because the ponies were the village's own, claimed by each family's notch, so nothing was taken from anyone.

P09.explanation: The officers took the bronzes and big canvases under a signed list, melted the bronzes into cannon, hung the canvases in the commander's headquarters, and refused to sell them back, so the army had "requisitioned" the collection: seized it officially for its own use. "Ransacked" fails because the pieces were crated, numbered and signed for, not rifled. "Ransomed" fails because the council offered to buy the pieces back and the army refused. "Repatriated" fails because the pieces went to the army's foundry and headquarters, not to the towns they had come from.

P10.explanation: Ships anchored beside the bar, crews landed cargo on its bare sand at low tide, and carts from town took it away and left goods for the ships, so the bar was where the port's goods changed hands: a "wharf." A "tollbooth" collects from traffic passing through, and a "turnstile" admits traffic one at a time, but the deep-sea ships never crossed the bar at all, and only fishing boats passed it to the piers. A "seawall" shelters a harbor, but winter swells rolled over the bar and broke against the town's piers.

P11.explanation: "Etched" fits: the stone under the ivy carries fine shallow grooves that follow the rootlets' paths and will not brush off, so the ivy cut marks into the wall's surface. "Dislodged" fails because stones on the ivy half stood as firm as on the bare half; the ivy marked the surface without moving any stone. "Dried" fails because moisture readings behind the leaves matched those on the bare half. "Fortified" fails because both halves stood in sound mortar and both survived the gale, so the ivy added no strength.

P12.explanation: "Annexed" fits: alliance officials took over the customs house, raised the alliance's flag and collected the port's duties for the alliance's treasury, so the alliance made the port its own. "Blockaded" fails because freighters still came and went. "Bombarded" fails because ships unloaded at the waterfront sheds as before, so the waterfront was standing. "Boycotted" fails because the alliance's buyers took more of the island's wool than ever.

P13.explanation: "Fence" fits: the wall closes the orchard in on every side with one locked gate, and the deer that strip young trees outside it leave the orchard's trees alone, so it keeps animals out. "Hearth" fails because frost blackens the blossom on the trees beside the wall as much as on any other, so the wall gives the orchard no warmth. "Dike" fails because the river lies a mile to the west, too far for the wall to hold back its water. "Firebreak" fails because the village fire crossed the common and burned the orchard's eastern rows despite the wall, so the wall did not stop fire.

P14.explanation: The monastery bought vellum and ink by the cartload, bishops paid it for service books, and most of the valley's surviving church books are in its monks' hand, so it was where the valley's books were written out: a "scriptorium." A "vault" keeps valuables safe, but every book it made left for the church that paid for it. A "tavern" serves travelers food and drink for pay, but travelers were fed at the gate one night free. A "sanatorium" takes in the sick, but even its own ill monks were carried down to the town's hospital.

P15.explanation: Miners left sealed pouches of gold dust and bundles of letters in the safe, marked with their names, and got them back with seals unbroken when they left, for a small fee, so the store was the camp's "repository": the place where its valuables were deposited for safekeeping. "Pawnshop" fails because the deposits came back sealed and whole for a keeping fee, so they were never security for a loan that could be forfeited. "Parlor" fails because the merchant barred the door at sundown. "Pharmacy" fails because the bottles held lamp oil and whiskey.

P16.explanation: "Battery" fits: the oil soaked into the bones is broken down so slowly that, thirty years on, it still powers the bacteria and the clams that feed on them, so the carcass stores energy and releases it steadily. "Banquet" fails because the community it supports has gone on for thirty years rather than ending in one feast. "Cupboard" fails because the energy reaches the clams through the bacteria that live on the bones; nothing is taken away by visitors. "Bridge" fails because young clams settle among their parents on the same bones, so the carcass is a lasting home rather than a link to somewhere else.

P17.explanation: Sand dropped by the current covered the ship to its mastheads within a decade, and divers had to pump away twelve feet of it to reach the deck, so three centuries of seawater had "interred" the ship, burying it. "Mummified" fails because the timbers had gone soft and black, so the sand kept the hull's shape without preserving its wood as it had been. "Mined" fails because the timbers were solid through, untouched by the boring worms that riddle wood left exposed on that coast. "Jostled" fails because the hull lay whole and in place under the sand.

P18.explanation: "Denuded" fits: the grazed slope holds a tenth of the plants on the other side, the few left survive in cracks the sheep cannot reach, and its soil has washed away, so the flock has stripped the hillside of its cover. "Groomed" fails because grooming leaves a neat, continuous turf, and this slope has almost no plants left to keep neat. "Fertilized" fails because the slope's soil tests no richer than the ungrazed slope's. "Furrowed" fails because the sheep wander in every direction and have worn no paths into it.

P19.explanation: "Flipped" fits: every feature is on the print at its true distance from its neighbors but in reverse order, west for east, which is what a drawing copied straight onto a copper plate produces, so the engraver reversed the survey. "Doctored" fails because nothing was singled out: every cape, bay, and shoal is present and keeps its exact spacing, and the whole coast is reversed by the plate, not altered here and there to mislead. "Enlarged" fails because the print is the survey's size. "Gilded" fails because the print's open sea is as bare of ornament as the survey's.

P20.explanation: Once the ants were banded off, caterpillars and beetles ate half the shrubs' leaves, while shrubs with ants on their stems at every hour lost almost none, so the ants "patrolled" the shrub, keeping leaf-eaters off it around the clock. "Pollinated" fails because banded shrubs flowered and podded as heavily without ants. "Propagated" fails because seeds of shrubs with and without ants alike dropped beneath the parent. "Parasitized" fails because the shrubs did better with the ants: banded shrubs, stripped of leaves, ended a third shorter.

P21.explanation: The lines name towns in order up the river with a number of days beside each, and each barley amount is exactly what twenty donkeys eat in that many days, under a caravan master's seal, so the tablet is the caravan master's "roadmap": the stages of his route with the feed each leg needs. "Receipt" fails because each amount is calculated from days of travel, a plan of what the donkeys will need, not a record of grain someone handed over. "Payroll" fails because the lines name towns, not workers. "Recipe" fails because the amounts are feed for stages of a journey, not quantities to be combined.

P22.explanation: Every issue went to a ministry office before printing and came back with its army stories struck out, so the government "muzzled" the press, stopping it from saying what it would have said. "Mobilized" fails because the editors left the struck columns blank instead of filling them, a visible refusal that readers read as the war news, so the papers were resisting the government, not working for it. "Nationalized" fails because the papers stayed with their founding families. "Impoverished" fails because their sales rose through the war.

P23.explanation: The flood left a thin film of dark silt, the unfertilized corn grew taller and darker than the crop on the higher field, and the topsoil's nitrogen nearly doubled, so the flood had "manured" the field, adding nutrients the way fertilizer does. "Mulched" fails because the silt was too thin to hide the furrows and the early-summer weeds came up thick, while a mulch smothers weeds under a real covering. "Leached" fails because the top foot of soil gained nitrogen rather than losing it. "Mired" fails because, soft as the silt was, the corn went in on schedule, so the field was never too wet to work.

P24.explanation: The floor is bare, polished and scratched, and the river from the melting ice carried silt as fine as talc into the lake below, so the glacier "milled" the valley floor, grinding its rock into powder and carrying it away. "Incised" fails because the grooves are scratches on a floor that is broad and even from wall to wall, so the ice cut no channel into it. "Littered" fails because no loose stone larger than a fist lies on the floor. "Mantled" fails because the floor is bare granite, and what the ice removed went downstream as silt into the lake rather than being spread over the floor.

P25.explanation: "Condemned" fits: engineers found the tower leaning and the walls cracked, and the building was fenced off and closed to everyone, so the council declared it unsafe. "Bulldozed" fails because the church still stands inside the fence. "Crated" fails because its bell and stained glass are still in place where it has always stood, so it was not taken apart and shipped away. "Commandeered" fails because no one has been allowed in or made any use of it, so the council did not take it over for its own purposes.

P26.explanation: "Dump" fits: the museum sent down works it had struck from its catalog and could not even sell, nobody listed them, and the chamber was walled up and never reopened, so the mine was where it got rid of them. "Depository" fails because a depository keeps things for their owner to retrieve; these works had been struck from the catalog, so the museum no longer counted them as its own, and they were sealed in without a list, put away for good rather than held for later. "Hospital" fails because the water-stained copies were leaned against the walls and bricked in, with no one ever working on them. "Gallery" fails because, although the paintings were set out in rows along the walls, the chamber was bricked up at once and has stayed shut, so no one ever saw them.

P27.explanation: The bow lies just under the surface at the edge of the only channel, unseen at low tide, and three later ships have torn their hulls open on it, so the hull is a hidden hazard that catches passing ships: a "tripwire." A "trellis" is a framework things grow along, but breaking surf keeps its plates bare. A "tomb" holds the dead, but the crew walked ashore the next morning. A "strongbox" keeps valuables secure, but its cargo of rails was hauled up and sold the next summer.

P28.explanation: Irrigation water soaked the clay beneath the road, the clay swelled, and the survey stakes stood higher each fall until the middle mile was a foot above its laid height, so the surface had been "raised". "Ruptured" fails because the asphalt rose in one long swell and stayed unbroken. "Rippled" fails because the rise was a single long swell, and the trucks braking at the stop sign, where folds would be shoved up, left no mark. "Rutted" fails because trucks crawling up the climb, where grooves would form, also left no mark.

P29.explanation: A wooded bank twenty feet high now stands unbroken between the highway and the homes, and families who kept their north windows shut for decades, against the traffic, now sleep with them open, so the park is the district's "muffler," deadening the highway's sound. "Magnet" fails because the two thousand daily visits are short trips by dog walkers from the blocks beside the park, so for all its traffic it draws no one from elsewhere. "Mixer" fails because those visitors come from the row-house blocks only, so the tower residents are not meeting their neighbors there. "Junction" fails because the bank is unbroken along the highway and the lawns slope down toward the homes, so no route runs through the park to anywhere beyond it.

P30.explanation: "Devoured" fits: once the honeydew ran low, the aphids on the ants' row disappeared by half in a week, leaving slit-open empty skins where they had been, while aphids the ants could not reach survived until frost, so the ants turned on the aphids and ate them. "Garnered" fails because the emptied skins lay on the leaves right where the clusters had been, so the aphids were consumed on the spot, not collected and stored. "Herded" fails because the ants never moved the aphids, not even off wilting shoots. "Drugged" fails because aphids walked as fast on ant-crossed leaves as on clean ones.

P31.explanation: The drought killed mostly the small, crowded pines, and the trees it left grew faster afterward than before, so it removed the weakest and left the strongest: it "winnowed" the forest. "Sapped" means drained of strength, but the survivors grew wider rings than before and beetles that prey on weakened pines found few hosts. "Scorched" means burned or browned at the surface, but the survivors kept green needles through every dry summer. "Toppled" means knocked over, but the dead trees stayed standing until they rotted.

P32.explanation: A well-known poet published poems that followed hers image by image and stanza by stanza, reworded and signed with his name alone, so her poems had been "plagiarized": their substance was passed off as his. "Pirated" fails because he did not reproduce her text; every line was reworded and set in his own collection, so no copy of her poems was printed and sold. "Panned" fails because the city papers had named two of her poems among the season's best. "Popularized" fails because her printer stopped at three hundred copies and his book sold about as many, so neither version carried the poems to a wide public.

P33.explanation: The race drew most of the stream off above the mill and sent it back only a mile downstream, leaving the bed between nearly dry, so the mill drew the stream's water away from its own channel: it "siphoned" the stream. "Stilled" means calmed the current, but a weir no higher than a boot backs up no pond, and below the outlet the current ran as fast as above the weir. "Soured" means fouled the water, but trout below the outlet were as many as in the next valley's streams. "Walled" means hemmed in with walls, but cattle crossed the bed anywhere along the drained mile.

P34.explanation: "Dredged" fits: for thirty years the beavers have scooped mud from the creek's pools and heaped it on the banks, leaving the pools three feet deeper than the creek next door, so they have cleared out their creek's bed. "Flooded" fails because there is no dam and the creek's level is unchanged, so no water spreads over the valley. "Deforested" fails because the slopes keep as many aspens as the next valley. "Greened" fails because in dry summers the valley turns just as brown as its neighbor.

P35.explanation: Three whole chapters are gone and a dozen sentences break off where pages were skipped, so the translator "mutilated" the novel, cutting it to pieces. "Lightened" fails because the chapters cut were the comic ones about the clowning uncle, while every drowning and winter of hunger stays in full, so the translation is darker than the original, not lighter. "Naturalized" fails because the family keeps its names, its fjord and its money. "Manicured" fails because the sentences keep the original's abrupt rhythm, and a dozen of them now stop mid-clause, which is the opposite of polish.

P36.explanation: The flat stones all tilted one way, each leaning on its downstream neighbor, and stayed in place through five floods, so the river had laid them one upon another: it had "stacked" them. "Sorted" means separated by size, but the sieved mix of sizes was the same at the cliffs as at the sea. "Stained" means given a color from outside, but a cracked stone showed the same shade inside as out. "Sanded" means worn down by grit, but even at the sea broken pebbles still fit back together edge to edge, so their edges had lost nothing.

P37.explanation: "Encrusted" fits: the hull sits exposed on rock where sea life can settle on it, and every surface carries a thick shell-and-coral coat over sound oak, so the two centuries have built a hard crust over the ship. "Entombed" fails because the ship is not sealed away: it rests on rock above the sand with its hatches open and fish passing through the hold, so the coat covers its surfaces without enclosing it. "Dismantled" fails because, for all the winter storms, the hull still lies whole where it came to rest. "Gnawed" fails because a core cut through the coat found the oak beneath still hard.

P38.explanation: Melting only in sunlight and draining down bare rock, the glacier makes the river rise at dusk and fall by dawn every summer day, and the mills grind from that evening rise until dawn, so it marks the time of day for the villages: it is the valley's "timepiece." A "storeroom" holds supplies for later use, but the glacier's daily rise is too small to fill the irrigation ditches, so the farms' summer water does not come from it. A "thermometer" registers temperature changes, but the front has stood at one ledge through warm decades and cold. A "signpost" points travelers along a route, but the glacier sits under cliffs that no road or path crosses.

P39.explanation: "Beached" fits: the gale drove the ships toward the coast, and at dawn they lay on the sand where their crews could walk around them, so the weather ran them ashore. "Capsized" fails because the ships lay upright and later floated off and sailed on. "Becalmed" fails because a gale drove them, so they had plenty of wind. "Blinded" fails because the night was moonlit, so the crews could see the coast coming; the gale, not poor visibility, put them on the sand.

P40.explanation: "Clogged" fits: with the spring floods held back, silt from a tributary settles in the channel, reeds root on the gravel bars, and side channels have filled in to become meadows, so the dam has let the river choke. "Bled" fails because the main channel runs deeper than before: the water that left the side channels is squeezed into the narrowed main channel, not taken away. "Chilled" fails because the water comes from the sunlit surface and bass, which need warm water, still spawn just below the dam. "Churned" fails because the dam releases a steady flow, which is why the silt can settle instead of being stirred away.
